passages.title: Clearing the blood by dialysis
paragraphs: In haemodialysis blood flows along one face of a synthetic membrane while dialysate flows the other way along the other. Solutes small enough to enter the pores diffuse down their own concentration gradients, each independently of the others, so the composition of the dialysate decides the direction in which every solute moves. The pores admit molecules up to about 10 kDa and exclude the plasma proteins altogether. By Fick's first law the diffusive flow of a solute is its diffusion coefficient in the membrane, multiplied by the membrane area and by the concentration difference across the membrane, divided by the membrane thickness. One widely used dialyser presents 1.6 m² of membrane 20 micrometres thick, and urea's diffusion coefficient in that membrane is 4.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s.

Table 1 lists the concentrations that a patient's blood and the prescribed dialysate carry as they enter the device. Urea and creatinine are absent from the dialysate, so they leave the blood as fast as diffusion allows. Potassium is held at 2.0 mM rather than at zero, because stripping it too quickly provokes arrhythmia. Bicarbonate is deliberately set above the blood's own value, and glucose is matched to the blood so that the treatment neither feeds nor starves the patient.

The proteins stay behind, and the osmotic pressure they exert holds water in the circulation. Plasma carries about 40 g/L of albumin, of molar mass 66,500 g/mol, and about 25 g/L of globulins, of average molar mass 150,000 g/mol. Treated as ideal solutes at 310 K they account for less than the 25 mmHg of colloid osmotic pressure actually measured in plasma, because each protein's negative charges hold a cloud of counterions that are themselves osmotically active.

Peritoneal dialysis dispenses with the machine and uses the peritoneum as the membrane. The dialysate instilled into the abdomen is made hypertonic, traditionally with 1.5 g of glucose per 100 mL, so that water is drawn out of the circulation across the membrane. Over a long dwell the glucose is itself absorbed, the gradient fades and water removal stalls; for overnight dwells a glucose polymer of about 4000 g/mol is used in its place.

passages.title: Reading a urine screen by GC-MS
paragraphs: An extract of urine is injected into a heated port, swept onto a narrow capillary column by a stream of helium, and carried through an oven whose temperature is raised on a programme. The inner wall of the column is coated with a thin film of a nonvolatile liquid, a nonpolar poly(dimethylsiloxane). A compound travels only while it is in the gas stream; every excursion into the liquid film holds it still, so the time it takes to reach the far end measures how strongly it partitions into the film. A compound that is retained not at all would emerge in 1.2 min on this column, the holdup time. The retention factor of a real analyte is the time the film held it back, divided by that holdup time. Polar, nonvolatile analytes are first converted to volatile derivatives, since a compound that will not evaporate cannot be carried at all.

At the far end the compounds pass into a mass spectrometer, where electrons at 70 eV knock an electron out of each molecule. Many of the resulting ions break apart, and the instrument separates all of them by mass divided by charge number. The most intense peak in the resulting spectrum is called the base peak, and it is not always the intact molecular ion. Table 1 lists the retention time, molecular mass and base peak of four compounds run as standards on this column.

Quantification uses an internal standard, the same compound labelled with deuterium, which is added to every sample at a fixed concentration. Because the labelled and unlabelled forms are extracted and injected with equal efficiency, the ratio of their peak areas depends on concentration alone. For amphetamine on this instrument the calibration line is ratio = 0.25 c + 0.05, with c in mg/L.

Neither measurement identifies a compound on its own. Hundreds of compounds appear in a urine extract, and a single column assigns many of them to the same narrow window of retention time. The mass spectrum supplies a second description of the same peak, and it is the pair together that a laboratory will defend.

passages.title: Separating serum proteins in an electric field
paragraphs: A drop of serum is applied near one end of a gel soaked in a buffer at pH 8.6, and 150 V is applied across the 10.0 cm between the electrodes. Every major serum protein has an isoelectric point below the buffer pH, so every one of them carries a net negative charge and all travel in the same direction, toward the anode. A protein reaches a steady speed almost at once, because the electric force on it is matched by the viscous drag of the gel. The electric force is the net charge times the field, and the drag is the Stokes drag, proportional to the buffer's viscosity, the protein's radius and its speed. Setting the two equal makes the steady speed proportional to the ratio of charge to radius, and the mobility, defined as that speed divided by the field, is a property of the protein and the buffer rather than of the voltage chosen.

Table 1 records the net charge and the Stokes radius of four serum proteins at pH 8.6, with the distance each travelled in a 30 min run. Albumin is both the most negative and among the smallest, and it leads the field; immunoglobulin G is nearly neutral at this pH and barely leaves the application point, which is why the immunoglobulins appear as a broad slow band rather than a sharp one.

Two practical limits bound the method. The current passing through the buffer heats the gel, and heat both distorts the bands and denatures the proteins, so the voltage cannot simply be raised until the run is quick. The buffer's ionic strength matters as well: a protein in a concentrated salt solution gathers a dense cloud of counterions of opposite sign, which screens part of its charge and lowers its mobility. Running at low ionic strength sharpens the separation but carries more of the current through the protein's own surroundings. Pushed much further, a high salt concentration takes the proteins out of solution altogether: this is how ammonium sulfate is used to precipitate albumin before a gel is ever run.

passages.title: A limb that swings like a pendulum
paragraphs: For much of the swing phase of walking, the leg hangs from the hip and moves largely without muscular driving, so the time it takes to swing forward can be predicted from mechanics alone. Two models are available. The first treats the leg as a simple pendulum, with all of its mass at the foot, a distance L from the pivot; its period is 2 π times the square root of L over g. The second treats it as a uniform rod pivoted at one end, whose mass is spread evenly along its length; its period is 2 π times the square root of 2L over 3g. Both results hold only for small angles, where the restoring torque is proportional to the displacement, and neither depends on the mass of the limb or on the size of the swing.

Four subjects of different height were filmed walking at the speed each chose freely. The swing time recorded for each is the time from the moment the foot leaves the ground to the moment it touches down again, which is half of a full pendulum period, since the leg swings forward and does not swing back before the foot lands. Table 1 lists leg length and swing time for the four. Take g as 9.8 m/s².

Walking near the limb's own pendulum period is cheap, because the muscles then supply only the small losses rather than the whole of the acceleration and deceleration. Walking faster than that, or carrying mass low on the leg, forces the hip flexors to drive the swing, and the metabolic cost per unit distance rises sharply. Within the small-angle limit, swinging the leg through a larger arc does not change the time the swing takes, since the larger arc is covered at a proportionally larger speed.

passages.title: Losing heat in a cool room
paragraphs: A resting adult turns about 80 W of chemical energy into heat, and an adult exercising hard can turn over 600 W. All of it has to leave the body, and it leaves by four routes. Heat is conducted outward through the shell of fat and skin, which can be modelled as a slab: the rate is the conductivity of the layer, times its area, times the temperature difference between its two faces, divided by its thickness. From the skin, heat passes to the surrounding air by convection, at a rate equal to a convective coefficient times the area times the difference between skin and air temperature. Heat also leaves as infrared radiation, and sweat carries heat away as it evaporates, each kilogram taking with it the latent heat of vaporisation.

Table 1 collects the quantities for one subject in a room at 22 °C, with skin at 33 °C and core at 37 °C. The slab model is a simplification in one important respect: most of the heat that reaches the skin in a warm subject is carried there by blood flowing through the dermis rather than conducted through the fat, and the body regulates its heat loss largely by opening and closing those vessels. The conductive estimate is therefore a floor on what the shell can pass when the skin vessels are shut.

Evaporation is the route that does not depend on the skin being warmer than the air. Sweat evaporates in proportion to the difference between the water vapour pressure at the wet skin and the water vapour pressure in the air, so it continues, and becomes the only route available, when the air is warmer than the body. In saturated air that difference nearly vanishes, and the sweat runs off without evaporating; this is why humid heat is dangerous at temperatures that dry heat is not.

passages.title: Designing a buffer for an injectable drug
paragraphs: A drug intended for injection hydrolyses quickly in acid and in alkali and is most stable near pH 5.0, losing less than two per cent of its potency a year between pH 4.5 and pH 5.5. The formulation therefore has to hold that window for the shelf life of the product, against acid released by the small amount of degradation that does occur and against carbon dioxide taken up through the closure. A weak acid and its conjugate base do this, and the pH they hold is given by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: the pH is the pKa of the acid plus the base-ten logarithm of the ratio of conjugate base to acid.

Two things decide which pair to use. The first is the pKa: capacity is greatest when the pH equals the pKa, where the two forms are present in equal amounts, and it falls away on either side, so a pair is useful only within about one unit of its pKa. The second is the total concentration, since capacity is proportional to it; but a concentrated buffer makes the injection hypertonic and stings at the injection site, so the formulation is held to 0.10 mol of buffer in total per litre. Table 1 lists the candidates available in injectable grade.

The chosen formulation is 1.0 L of solution containing 0.10 mol of acetic acid and sodium acetate between them, adjusted to pH 5.00. Buffer capacity can be quantified as the moles of strong acid that a litre absorbs per unit fall in pH over a small addition, and it depends on the total concentration of the pair and on how evenly the pair is divided between its two forms.

passages.title: Making a drug intermediate by aldol condensation
paragraphs: A conjugated enone used as a drug intermediate is made by condensing benzaldehyde with acetophenone in aqueous ethanol containing sodium hydroxide. Hydroxide removes the slightly acidic hydrogen from the carbon next to acetophenone's carbonyl group, giving an enolate whose negative charge is shared between that carbon and the oxygen. The carbon end attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde, which joins the two fragments by a new carbon-carbon bond and gives a beta-hydroxy ketone. That alcohol then loses water across the two carbons between the new bond and the carbonyl, leaving a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with both the carbonyl group and a benzene ring. Benzaldehyde has no hydrogen on a carbon next to its own carbonyl, so it cannot form an enolate and cannot condense with itself, which is what keeps the pairing clean.

Three runs were made with each substrate at 0.20 M. Trial 1, in 1.0 M sodium hydroxide at 25 °C for two hours, gave 86 per cent of the enone and 5 per cent of the beta-hydroxy ketone. Trial 2, in 0.010 M sodium hydroxide at 0 °C for two hours, gave 20 per cent of the enone and 62 per cent of the beta-hydroxy ketone. Trial 3, with no base at 25 °C for two hours, returned the starting materials unchanged.

The enone is favoured thermodynamically because its double bond is conjugated with the carbonyl group and the ring, and the dehydration can be pushed further by distilling water out of the mixture. The molar masses needed for a yield calculation are 106 g/mol for benzaldehyde, 120 g/mol for acetophenone, 226 g/mol for the beta-hydroxy ketone and 208 g/mol for the enone.

passages.title: How much of an X-ray beam gets through
paragraphs: A narrow beam of X-ray photons crossing matter is attenuated exponentially: the fraction transmitted is e raised to minus the product of the linear attenuation coefficient of the material and the thickness crossed. Each layer removes the same fraction of whatever reaches it, so the thickness that halves the beam, the half-value layer, is the natural logarithm of 2 divided by the attenuation coefficient. Doubling the thickness therefore squares the transmitted fraction rather than halving it.

At the energies used for diagnosis the dominant interaction in a heavy element is the photoelectric effect, whose probability per atom rises roughly with the cube of atomic number and falls steeply as photon energy rises. In the light elements of soft tissue, Compton scattering from loosely bound outer electrons contributes most of the attenuation instead, and it depends on electron density rather than on atomic number. The difference is what gives a radiograph its contrast: bone attenuates far more than the muscle around it chiefly because of the calcium in it, and a contrast agent works by carrying iodine or barium into a soft tissue. Table 1 gives measured coefficients at 60 keV, a typical mean energy for a diagnostic beam.

The same figures govern shielding and filtration. A sheet of aluminium placed in the beam removes the lowest-energy photons preferentially, since the photoelectric cross-section falls with energy; those photons would have been absorbed in the patient's skin without ever reaching the detector, so filtering them out lowers the dose without dimming the image. Lead is reserved for shielding, where the aim is to stop everything in the least thickness possible.

passages.title: How fast cells settle in plasma
paragraphs: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is measured by standing a column of anticoagulated blood upright and reading how far the boundary between clear plasma and settled cells has fallen after one hour. A single cell settling in plasma reaches a steady speed within a fraction of a second, at which its weight is balanced by the buoyant force and by the viscous drag. For a sphere in a laminar flow, Stokes' law makes that speed twice the square of the radius, times the difference in density between particle and fluid, times g, divided by nine times the viscosity of the fluid. A red cell is treated here as an equivalent sphere of radius 3.5 micrometres and density 1098 kg/m³; plasma has a density of 1025 kg/m³ and, when healthy, a viscosity of 1.5 mPa s, against 1.0 mPa s for water.

What makes the measurement useful in illness is that fibrinogen and the other acute-phase proteins make red cells stack face to face into rouleaux. An aggregate settles as one body, so the effective radius in Stokes' law rises, and because the speed goes as the square of the radius, a modest degree of stacking raises the rate steeply. The same proteins also thicken the plasma, which acts in the opposite direction. Table 1 lists the plasma viscosity, the effective aggregate radius and the measured rate for four patients.

Two assumptions in the law are worth holding in mind. It describes laminar flow around the particle, which is amply satisfied here: the Reynolds number for a settling cell is of order ten to the minus five, so inertia plays no part. It also describes an isolated particle, which real blood is not. A high cell count means neighbouring cells and the upward flow of displaced plasma hinder each other, which slows the settling; this is why anaemia raises the measured rate and why polycythaemia lowers it.

passages.title: Reading an inhibitor off a double-reciprocal plot
paragraphs: An enzyme assayed over a range of substrate concentrations gives an initial rate that rises steeply at low substrate and flattens toward a maximum rate at high substrate. Taking the reciprocal of both the rate and the substrate concentration turns that curve into a straight line: a plot of one over the rate against one over the substrate concentration has a slope equal to the Michaelis constant divided by the maximum rate, and it meets the vertical axis at one over the maximum rate. Two quantities can therefore be read off a fitted line, and the slope divided by the intercept returns the Michaelis constant on its own.

The plot also sorts inhibitors by what they leave untouched. An inhibitor that competes with the substrate for the same site can always be out-competed by raising the substrate concentration, so the maximum rate, and with it the vertical intercept, is unchanged, while the apparent Michaelis constant and the slope both rise. An inhibitor that binds elsewhere and lowers the maximum rate raises the intercept instead. For a competitive inhibitor the apparent Michaelis constant is the true one multiplied by the quantity one plus the inhibitor concentration divided by the inhibition constant.

Table 1 gives the reciprocal rates measured at four substrate concentrations, with and without 10 micromolar of a candidate drug. Rates are in micromol per litre per minute and substrate concentrations in millimolar, so the reciprocal rates carry units of litre minutes per micromol. The apparent Michaelis constant in the presence of the drug is 6.0 mM.
